A litigant is any person — or organisation — who is directly involved in a lawsuit in a court of law. That's it at the heart. If you are part of a legal case being fought in court, you are a litigant.

The key word here is directly. A litigant is not the judge, not the lawyer, not a witness. A litigant is one of the people the fight is actually between — the ones with something at stake in the outcome of the case.

Think of a lawsuit like a formal, legal argument taken to a court. Two sides disagree about something — maybe money, property, a contract, an injury, or a right — and they cannot settle it themselves, so they bring it before a judge.

Every person on either side of that argument is a litigant.
The Two Sides of a Litigant

In any lawsuit, there are generally two opposing sides, and litigants fall into one of them:

1. The Plaintiff
This is the litigant who started the lawsuit. They are the one who felt wronged, harmed, or cheated and decided to take legal action. For example, if your neighbour damages your car and refuses to pay, and you take them to court — you are the plaintiff litigant.

2. The Defendant
This is the litigant who is being sued. They are the one the lawsuit is brought against. In the same example, your neighbour — the one being taken to court — is the defendant litigant.

Both the plaintiff and the defendant are litigants. The word "litigant" applies equally to both sides, without taking sides.

A litigant does not have to be a single human being. The word applies to:

  • Individual people — a person suing their employer, or a person being sued by their landlord.
  • Companies and businesses — a company suing another company over a broken contract.
  • Organisations — a charity, a government body, a union, etc.
  • Groups of people — in what's called a class action lawsuit, a large group of people collectively become litigants together.

So any legal party to a lawsuit — human or non-human entity — can be called a litigant.

This is important for sharp understanding:

  • A lawyer (attorney) is not a litigant. They represent the litigant, but they are not the one whose interests are at stake. They go home the same regardless of who wins.
  • A judge is not a litigant. They are the neutral decision-maker.
  • A witness is not a litigant. They appear in court to give testimony, but they are not a party to the dispute.
  • A mediator or arbitrator is not a litigant. They help resolve disputes but are not personally involved in the conflict.

A litigant is always one of the parties in conflict — never someone playing a supporting role in the court.
A Special Kind: The "Pro Se" Litigant

Sometimes, a litigant chooses to fight their legal case without hiring a lawyer — they represent themselves in court. This person is called a pro se litigant (sometimes also called a self-represented litigant). This is perfectly legal in most countries, though it is considered very difficult because legal proceedings are complex. You'll come across this term often in legal writing.
The Broader Context — When Is Someone Called a Litigant?

The word "litigant" is used almost exclusively in formal, legal contexts. You won't hear it in casual conversation. It appears in:

  • Court documents and legal filings
  • News reports about lawsuits
  • Legal textbooks and journals
  • Judgements written by judges

You would say: "The litigant filed a motion with the court" or "Both litigants were present at the hearing."
When Does Someone Stop Being a Litigant?

A person is a litigant only for the duration of the legal proceedings. Once the case is resolved — whether by a court verdict, a settlement, an appeal being exhausted, or the case being dropped — the litigation is over, and technically, so is their status as a litigant in that particular case.
A Concrete Example to Tie It All Together

Imagine this: Sarah buys a used car from a dealership. The dealer told her the car was in perfect condition, but it breaks down the very next day. She discovers the dealer knew about a serious engine defect and hid it. She decides to sue.

  • Sarah is the litigant (plaintiff) — she brought the case to court.
  • The dealership is the litigant (defendant) — they are being sued.
  • Sarah's lawyer is not a litigant — they are her legal representative.
  • The judge presiding over the case is not a litigant.
  • A mechanic who testifies about the engine defect is not a litigant — they are a witness.

Both Sarah and the dealership are litigants because they are the two parties with a direct stake in the outcome of the lawsuit.
A litigant is any person or organisation who is an active party — either suing or being sued — in a court case, and who has a direct personal or financial stake in the outcome of that legal dispute.
